guides.title: Lucy and her world
guides.description: A 3.2-million-year-old skeleton from Hadar, and the fossils and footprints that help explain how her species moved.
guides.intro: On November 24, 1974, Donald Johanson and Tom Gray found the first fragments of a remarkably complete skeleton at Hadar in Ethiopia’s Afar region. Known as Lucy and as Dinkinesh in Amharic, and catalogued as AL 288-1, she lived about 3.2 million years ago. Her bones connect the story of discovery to a much older story of walking on two legs.

paragraphs.text: Johanson and Gray were returning from a survey when they spotted a fragment of arm bone. The search recovered parts of the skull, trunk, pelvis and limbs, together representing about 40 percent of an individual skeleton by bone count. Lucy was assigned to Australopithecus afarensis, a species named for the Afar.

November 1974 is the date of discovery. Lucy’s geological age of just under 3.18 million years comes from the position of her bones within Hadar’s layers. Radiometric ages from volcanic deposits, alongside magnetic and fossil evidence, place the skeleton in the Kada Hadar Member.

Lucy’s fused bones and erupted wisdom teeth indicate an adult. The National Museum of Ethiopia in Addis Ababa holds the original fossil. Researchers can study and exhibit casts made from molds of the bones.

Lucy’s pelvis, thigh and knee preserve the alignment and joint structure of a biped. In combination, bones from the same skeleton bring more information about how she moved than a single fossil joint could provide. The species retained features, including curved finger bones, consistent with climbing.

At Laetoli, the Site G footprints record actual steps in volcanic sediment. They predate Lucy by almost half a million years, and their usual attribution to Australopithecus afarensis rests on the track anatomy and the fossils found at Laetoli. An unusual neighboring trail from Site A suggests another form of bipedal gait.

At Dikika, the juvenile skeleton known as Selam preserves anatomy Lucy’s remains leave incomplete. The Dikika team reported a lower limb consistent with bipedality and upper-body traits relevant to climbing. The fossil belongs to the same species and is slightly older than Lucy.

At Woranso-Mille, the 2025 description of teeth and jaws supported assigning a foot from Burtele to Australopithecus deyiremeda. Its grasping big toe points to a different mix of climbing and upright walking in a probable contemporary of Lucy’s species. Several kinds of hominins shared the Afar landscape across this interval.

Australopithecus afarensis is a candidate for an ancestral population of later hominins. Comparing multiple species and their ages is essential, because the older skeleton of an upright walker by itself leaves open which population gave rise to Homo. Lucy provides unusually detailed evidence of one individual on that branching history.

guides.intro: The oldest possible members of the human lineage are millions of years older than Lucy. Later, Australopithecus and Paranthropus overlapped with early Homo, and several populations of Homo shared parts of Eurasia. Fossils document this diversity. DNA from later groups also shows where branches met again.

paragraphs.text: Hominins include living humans and extinct species more closely related to us than to chimpanzees and bonobos. Near the split, researchers compare such clues as tooth form, the base of the skull and anatomy related to bipedal movement. An isolated bone or tooth can fit more than one evolutionary interpretation.

A fossil’s age establishes a known occurrence in a particular region. The lineage may have originated earlier or elsewhere. A type specimen anchors a scientific name, and an older find assigned to that name can change the first occurrence. Ma means million years ago and ka means thousand years ago.

sections.heading: Late Miocene and early Pliocene candidates

paragraphs.text: Toros-Menalla, the Tugen Hills and the Middle Awash preserve different parts of the earliest fossil record. The 2026 study of limb fragments from Chad strengthens a bipedal interpretation for Sahelanthropus, while the fragmentary remains and disagreements over their anatomy leave its place near the hominin split open.

cells: Mandible and upper fourth premolar showing fused root canals interpreted by Fuss et al. (2017) as hominin-like; whether it is an earliest hominin or a late Miocene Eurasian ape remains actively debated.
Fossils are documented from TM 247, TM 266 and TM 292. TM 266 yielded the Toumaï cranium and limb bones attributed to this species. The localities cannot be securely ranked by age.
The original small corpus came from Aragai, Cheboit, Kapcheberek and Kapsomin. Femur shape has been interpreted as evidence of bipedality.

The Middle Awash cluster includes Alayla, Asa Koma, Saitune Dora and Amba East. A toe bone is consistent with bipedality. Teeth from nearby Gona, some possibly as old as 6.3 Ma, are attributed to Ardipithecus kadabba or to an unidentified early hominin.
Gona’s fossil ages overlap the roughly 4.4 Ma Aramis assemblage. The more complete Aramis skeleton preserves evidence relevant to both climbing and bipedal movement.
Later or overlapping finds include Asa Issie in the Middle Awash, Allia Bay in Kenya and the 3.8 Ma Woranso-Mille cranium in Ethiopia.

paragraphs.text: The Ethiopian fossils suggest possible overlap between late Australopithecus anamensis and early Australopithecus afarensis. The latter coexisted in the broader East African region with forms given other names, among them Australopithecus deyiremeda and Kenyanthropus platyops. Comparisons of teeth and feet help assess how these populations differed in diet and locomotion.

Paranthropus is the name commonly used for several hominins with specialized chewing anatomy. At Nyayanga, two teeth place the genus early on the Homa Peninsula. Their association with Oldowan artifacts leaves open whether Paranthropus, another hominin or more than one group used the stone technology there.

sections.heading: Early Homo in Africa and Eurasia

paragraphs.text: A fragmentary lower jaw from Ledi-Geraru is the oldest widely cited fossil assigned to Homo. At different localities in the same research area, fossils document Homo around 2.78 and 2.59 Ma and an unnamed Australopithecus around 2.63 Ma. Together with Paranthropus at Mille-Logya around 2.6 Ma, the finds place several lineages in the Afar during this interval.

Shangchen and Dmanisi illustrate why fossil dates and activity dates deserve separate entries. Shangchen’s older stone horizons have no identified makers. The oldest tools at Dmanisi predate the main skeleton-bearing layer there, which contains multiple individuals whose variation has invited different species names.

The known sample comes from Gran Dolina’s TD6. Older Homo at nearby Sima del Elefante has a different, tentative assignment. Enamel proteins place antecessor near the ancestry of later Homo lineages without identifying a direct ancestor.

paragraphs.text: Later fossils are still difficult to place in a single tree. The name Homo heidelbergensis has been applied narrowly to specimens resembling the Mauer mandible or more broadly to several Middle Pleistocene populations. Other fossils reveal local branches, such as the small-bodied hominins on Flores and the cave finds on Luzon.

The fossils combine a relatively modern face with an older-looking braincase. At Omo Kibish in Ethiopia, Omo I predates an ash layer dated to 233 ± 22 ka. These finds record early populations across Africa.

sections.heading: Denisovans and the evidence for contact

paragraphs.text: Denisovans are a late branch of the human family, first identified through DNA from Denisova Cave. The oldest well-contextualized Denisovan fossils there date to about 200 ka, and cave sediment preserves their mitochondrial DNA in older deposits. Lucy lived about 3.2 Ma and the earliest candidate hominins date to around 7 Ma. The known age of a fossil or sediment sample also differs from the time its lineage separated from another.

Denisovans and Neanderthals are closely related lineages. A bone fragment at Denisova Cave yielded the genome of a girl with a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father. Denisovan-derived DNA in some living people records other encounters, including with ancestors of present-day populations in Oceania. The molecular lineage spans fossils assigned different species names, including the Harbin cranium originally named Homo longi. Proposed names and the range of fossils they cover remain debated.

sections.heading: What genetic and molecular evidence can establish

paragraphs.text: Ancient DNA is a physical trace from a particular specimen, but turning it into a population history requires comparison and modelling. Researchers test contamination, fragment damage and consistency across extracts, then compare patterns across many sites in the genome. A resemblance at one position is weaker evidence than a consistent genome-wide pattern.

The categories below answer different questions. A protein-based lineage assignment, a maternal genealogy and a genome-wide admixture estimate should never be presented as interchangeable measurements.

cells: Many inherited regions from both parents can identify close kinship, population affinities and introgressed segments.
Sequenced individuals remain a small sample; estimated contact dates depend on generation lengths, recombination and demographic assumptions.
A largely maternally inherited genealogy, often recoverable when nuclear DNA is scarce.
One maternal line is not the whole family tree. Sima nuclear DNA is Neanderthal-related although its mitochondrial affinity is Denisovan-related.
Surviving amino-acid variants can place fossils near a lineage beyond the usual DNA preservation window.
A small set of proteins cannot substitute for a whole genome or normally measure a person’s genome-wide admixture fraction.
Anatomical comparisons, dating and geographic presence; tools document behavior.
A mosaic of traits is not by itself proof of interbreeding, and tools do not necessarily identify their makers.

sections.heading: Interbreeding: a child, recent ancestors and older gene flow

paragraphs.text: Denisova 11 is unusually direct evidence. Slon and colleagues (2018) found the genome-wide pattern expected for a first-generation daughter of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father. Her father also carried older Neanderthal ancestry. This establishes parentage for one individual; it does not reveal where her parents met or whether she later had children.

Oase 1 from Romania supplies a different kind of evidence. Fu and colleagues (2015) inferred a Neanderthal ancestor roughly four to six generations back from very long inherited segments. Their estimate of about 6–9% Neanderthal ancestry describes this approximately 42–37-thousand-year-old individual, not all early Europeans.

For older contact, recombination breaks inherited segments into shorter pieces across generations. Iasi and colleagues (2024) modelled most shared Neanderthal gene flow in their samples within an extended interval about 50.5–43.5 thousand years ago. Sümer and colleagues, published online in 2024, obtained approximately 49–45 thousand years from early European genomes. Different models and samples give related estimates, not an exact date for every encounter.

Introgressed DNA persisting in later populations demonstrates that at least some mixed descendants reproduced. It does not mean every pairing was fertile or that the lineages had no barriers to gene flow. Species names remain classifications; limited interbreeding and long-term genetic differentiation can coexist.

The comparisons below refer to sampled people and published analyses. They are not fixed racial percentages or properties of everyone living in a region. Later migration, population mixing, selection and the choice of reference genomes change both the distribution of ancestry and its estimated amount. Modern sample locations also do not locate prehistoric encounters.

cells: Iasi et al. (2024) summarize roughly 1–2% Neanderthal ancestry for most present-day people with ancestry outside Africa.
Individual histories vary; early people such as Oase had much higher recent contributions and are not an average for the region.
Neanderthal ancestry is widespread; studies also detect Denisovan-derived segments with more than one affinity to the Altai genome.
Some methods estimate more Neanderthal sequence than in European samples. The size of that difference depends on reference choice and demographic modelling.
Denisovan-derived ancestry occurs in sampled populations, generally at lower levels than in the Papuan comparison samples.
Broad regional labels conceal differences among groups and histories; a detectable segment is not a separate species identity.

The early estimate is study-specific. Papuans, Aboriginal Australians and all Pacific Islanders cannot be assigned one universal value.

A selected locus can be common without a similarly high genome-wide ancestry fraction; the fossil and admixture histories are separate questions.

These are competing demographic explanations, not a confirmed fossil species assignment or one percentage for Africa.

sections.heading: Africa: back-migration and unresolved deep ancestry

paragraphs.text: Africa has its own complex population history. Chen and colleagues (2020) used a method that does not require a supposedly unadmixed modern African reference. Their results support movement back into Africa by people whose ancestors had acquired Neanderthal ancestry in Eurasia. They also show that older gene flow from early modern humans into Neanderthals can produce sequence sharing. Neither process requires Neanderthals themselves to have lived at the location of a present-day African sample.

An additional question concerns deep ancestry without a matching ancient genome. Durvasula and Sankararaman (2020) inferred gene flow from an unsampled divergent population in four West African datasets. Their model-dependent ancestry estimates had a broad 2–19% range across analyses. That range is not a measured universal African fraction, and the study cannot identify the source as H. naledi, H. erectus or another named fossil species.

Ragsdale and colleagues (2023) tested a wider set of histories, including new Nama genomes alongside eastern and western African comparisons. Models with weakly differentiated ancestral populations exchanging genes for long periods explained signals previously attributed to a sharply separated archaic source. This does not prove that all archaic contact was absent; it shows that a genetic pattern can have more than one plausible demographic explanation.

sections.heading: Sampling, percentages and the missing branches

paragraphs.text: Ancient genomes are unevenly preserved and sampled. A sequenced Altai Denisovan is a reference individual, not a complete representation of Denisovan diversity. Browning et al. (2018) and Jacobs et al. (2019) found patterns inconsistent with a single uniform Denisovan source. Dates, number of contacts and inferred source relationships can change when new genomes are added.

Analyses also differ in which sites they measure. Iasi et al. (2024) found that a commonly used ancient-DNA capture panel contained too few archaic-informative sites for their intended ancestry analysis and selected suitable genome or capture datasets. A reported percentage therefore needs its method and comparison samples, not just a population label.

Proteins extend the molecular record: Homo antecessor enamel gives information much older than most hominin DNA. But limited protein variation can leave relationships unresolved. For many named fossil lineages, including the early australopiths and the island taxa, we lack genomes that could directly test particular interbreeding claims. No recovered DNA is not evidence that no contact occurred; equally, possible contact is not demonstrated gene flow.

Genome-wide ancestry and particular inherited variants also behave differently. Selection can favor an advantageous variant such as the Denisovan-like EPAS1 haplotype while other introgressed regions are lost. A variant’s present frequency does not measure the number of ancient encounters or a person’s overall ancestry.

sections.heading: What became of the other lineages?

paragraphs.text: A lineage can disappear as a distinct population while some of its ancestry continues in another. Neanderthal and Denisovan DNA in later humans demonstrates partial genetic survival. It does not show that every local group was absorbed, identify a single cause of disappearance, or establish that an ancient individual with no detected contribution to sampled people had no descendants at all.

The final known fossil is a minimum record of how late a lineage existed, not the date its last member died. The dated Ngandong bone bed records H. erectus at about 117–108 thousand years ago. Revised Liang Bua dates place H. floresiensis bones around 100–60 thousand years ago; whether the lineage survived later remains open.

Denisovan history also differs by place. The 2025 Denisova Cave synthesis records changes in maternal lineages and late local evidence around 55 thousand years ago, while the Baishiya rib occurs in a layer dated about 48–32 thousand years ago. Neither site supplies a global extinction date. Naledi and luzonensis have still more limited geographic records; their disappearance and any genetic legacy remain unresolved.

For the much earlier branches, fossils document diversity, overlap and anatomical change, while their exact relationships remain debated. A chronological sequence on this map is not a claim that each named species transformed into the next. Missing markers reflect the selected evidence and preservation record, not an empty continent.

sections.heading: Genetic drift and the serial founder effect across continents

paragraphs.text: Every time a small pioneering band budded off to settle new terrain outside Africa, it carried only a random subset of its parent population's genetic variants—a bottleneck known as the serial founder effect. Across 142 to 929 sequenced global populations, neutral genetic diversity (heterozygosity) falls smoothly with overland walking distance from sub-Saharan Africa, while genetic drift randomly magnifies differences between separated regions.

Because African populations remained larger and older with no single Out-of-Africa bottleneck, two African communities (such as Khoe-San hunter-gatherers and West African farmers) often differ more in deep genetic lineages than Europeans do from East Asians or Aboriginal Australians.

sections.heading: Did Aboriginal Australians end up very different from Europeans and Indigenous Americans?

paragraphs.text: Yes—in deep lineage divergence, isolation duration, and archaic heritage, Indigenous Australians stand conspicuously distinct from both Europeans and Indigenous Americans. Once ancestors of Australians and Papuans split from Eurasian lineages ~58–50 ka and crossed Wallacea into Pleistocene Sahul, they experienced ~45,000 years of continental genetic isolation from Eurasia, amplified further by strong internal drift across Australia's arid central deserts.

At the same time, it is crucial to keep scale clear: all living humans remain ~99.9% identical across shared functional DNA, and non-Africans all stem from the same Out-of-Africa radiation (~70–55 ka). What separates Australia, Europe, and the Americas are three radically different post-exit demographic histories: ~45 millennia of Sahul isolation + dual Denisovan pulses (Australia/PNG), three massive Holocene homogenization waves (Europe), and a late Beringian bottleneck fusing East Asian and Ancient North Eurasian ancestors (Americas).

sections.heading: Europe's three-wave merger vs. the Beringian standstill

paragraphs.text: Europe's present-day genome is surprisingly young: 1,600+ ancient Eurasian genomes show that Mesolithic Western Hunter-Gatherers (WHG) were transformed first by incoming Anatolian Neolithic farmers (~7000–4000 BCE) and then again by Pontic–Caspian Yamnaya steppe herders (~3000 BCE).

Remarkably, those Yamnaya herders carried high proportions of Ancient North Eurasian (ANE) ancestry related to ~24 ka Siberian Mal'ta—meaning Native Americans (whose ancestors absorbed ~30–40% ANE alongside East Asians before crossing Beringia) share distant ~15–20% genomic kinship with modern Europeans despite opposite geographic ends of Eurasia.

sections.heading: Population Y, ghost lineages and adaptive archaic genes worldwide

paragraphs.text: Subtle archaic-and-regional exceptions enrich every continent: in Amazonia (Suruí, Karitiana) and ancient Lagoa Santa remains, a ~1–2% Australo-Melanesian affinity ('Population Y') reflects deep Asian/Beringian population structure surviving south of Panama; across Tibet, Denisovan *EPAS1* confers high-altitude hypoxia resilience; and across Europe, Asia, the Americas, and Oceania, archaic Neanderthal and Denisovan immune and mucosal variants (*TLR*, *HLA*, *MUC19*) underwent positive natural selection.

sections.heading: How to read an early trace

paragraphs.text: Footprints document movement across a surface. Refitted flakes and cores preserve parts of a stoneworking sequence. Cut marks and wear can connect tools to activities such as carcass processing. A fossil hominin records a body, while attribution of a nearby artifact to its species requires additional evidence.
Ma means million years ago. Dates refer to the ancient track, object-bearing deposit or earliest dated horizon described in each guide. Some ages are central estimates within wide ranges.

sections.heading: Stoneworking before the earliest known Homo

paragraphs.text: Lomekwi 3’s stone artifacts are older than the oldest fossil currently assigned to Homo. Nyayanga’s Oldowan layers include Paranthropus teeth, and Namorotukunan preserves early Oldowan horizons across changes in its landscape. The molecular and anatomical evidence needed to assign the tools to a particular species is usually absent.

At Dikika, researchers reported two animal bones with marks they interpreted as evidence of butchery more than 3.39 million years ago. Other kinds of damage can mimic tool marks, and no tools were recovered with those bones. The two marked bones are discussed here as a disputed line of evidence.

The long sequence at Shangchen documents repeated presence in central China. Dmanisi independently records an early dispersal with both tools and hominin remains. And Lokalalei 2C in Kenya, roughly contemporary with the early Shungura record, is especially informative about the production of flakes because pieces can be refitted.

guides.title: Laetoli footprint trails
guides.description: Footprints in volcanic ash document upright walking about 3.66 million years ago.
guides.intro: The Laetoli trackways in northern Tanzania preserve individual steps. The feet that made them are long gone, but the prints record how hominins moved across a volcanic surface during the Pliocene.

points.label: Laetoli footprint trails

paragraphs.text: At Site G, a sequence of impressions preserves a forward-facing big toe and a repeated pattern of steps on two feet. The trackway captures locomotion directly, whereas a fossil foot preserves anatomy from which gait has to be inferred.

The impressions occur in layers of volcanic tuff dated to about 3.66 million years ago. The age describes the ancient crossing. Site G was excavated in 1978, and a nearby set of prints at Site S was reported decades later.

The Site G tracks are usually attributed to Australopithecus afarensis, which is also represented by fossils at Laetoli. Re-excavation and comparison of the Site A trail suggested a different pattern of bipedal walking. The identity of that trackmaker remains uncertain.

guides.description: Early Oldowan artifacts, processed animal bones and Paranthropus teeth occur on Kenya’s Homa Peninsula.
guides.intro: Close to Lake Victoria, Nyayanga preserves evidence of Oldowan food processing well before 2.5 million years ago. The animal bones provide a way to ask how the implements were used, while two hominin teeth raise a separate question about who used them.

paragraphs.text: The assemblage includes cores and sharp flakes concentrated in a single buried horizon. Scar patterns record how pieces were removed, and the researchers used quantitative comparisons with Lomekwi and other Oldowan sites to evaluate the way the stone was worked.

The artifact horizon falls above a dated volcanic tuff and below a change in recorded magnetic polarity. These constraints give an interval of about 2.61–2.58 million years. The bracket overlaps the oldest evidence at nearby Gona at the scale of geological uncertainty.

The mandibular fossil and the younger tool horizon answer different questions about the same landscape.

sections.heading: Artifacts in loess and old soils

Magnetic minerals retain information about the polarity of Earth’s field when sediments formed. At Shangchen, polarity changes and regional correlations assign the oldest artifact-bearing beds to about 2.12 million years ago. Other levels extend the record forward to roughly 1.26 million years ago.

Placing Shangchen, Chinese Loess Plateau in human-family chronology depends on bracketing stratified volcanic ash layers (40Ar/39Ar), cosmogenic nuclide burial ages, or paleomagnetic reversals above and below the artifact or footprint horizon rather than dating stone flakes in isolation. Reworking, fluvial transport, and cut-mark/percussion equifinality remain key variables evaluated in every new study.

Rather than identifying a single exclusive ancestor, this locality serves as a tightly constrained chronological anchor that must be compared side-by-side with contemporary Rift, southern, north African, and Eurasian finds inside the playable Human Family map.
